title: Thumb-sized Hanuman
hookLine: with her mouth a hundred yojanas wide, Hanuman wins by becoming the size of a thumb and bowing; why the strongest god kneels
carry: make the ego small: Hanuman bows

lines: A MOUTH A HUNDRED YOJANAS WIDE.
cards: Out over the open sea, a monkey grown to the size of a mountain hangs in the air. In front of him, a serpent mother's jaws gape a hundred yojanas wide.
Every time he has grown, Surasa's mouth has grown wider, and the gods are watching. He's been answering size with size. Now, Valmiki says, in the blink of an eye, he does the opposite.

teach.b: Hanuman makes himself tiny, about the size of a thumb. He darts into Surasa's enormous mouth and, before she can close it, darts back out. Then he stops in the air, bows, and speaks respectfully.

teach.h: IN AND OUT; HER BOON IS KEPT.
teach.b: I've entered your mouth, so your boon is kept. Now I'm going on to find Sita. He hasn't broken her rule or his promise to Rama.
Surasa is delighted. She sets aside the frightening form, appears as herself, and blesses him: go, find Sita, bring her and Rama together. The gods who set the test cheer.
Many teachers read the scene this way: the ego, ahamkara, answers size with size, and that contest never ends. The devotee gets through by becoming small and bowing.

It's why the strongest being in the Ramayana is so often pictured kneeling at Rama's feet, hands folded. The Chalisa praises him for it: a tiny form to show himself to Sita, a terrible form to burn Lanka.
He knows which one the moment needs. Look back at the week of crossings. Jambavan told Hanuman his own story, as the Chalisa still does.
He went as Rama's arrow: dasya. The trees saw him off: ashirvad. He kept his sankalpa past Mainaka, who was repaying an old rina.
And with Surasa: strength, wisdom, and an ego small enough to bow. One more meeting waits over the sea, and it is not a test.

how: Many Hindu tellers, from grandparents to temple storytellers, use Surasa's test to show that Hanuman's wisdom matters as much as his strength; temple images often show him kneeling at Rama's feet with folded hands, and devotional art shows the tiny Hanuman beside her vast mouth.

games.q: Sam asks why the strongest god in the temple is kneeling with folded hands. by today's story, what fits?
o: he's the strongest, and his ego is the smallest: he bows, like he did to Surasa.
he lost a fight once and has to kneel.

games.why: Hanuman shrank, passed through Surasa's mouth and bowed. devotees picture him kneeling at Rama's feet: great strength, small ego.

practice: Fold your hands and bow your head a little, the way Hanuman bowed to Surasa, and the way many Hindus bow before a murti. Let your breathing become small and quiet: shoulders soft, no need to take up extra room.
If a thought pushes in, don't push back; let it pass through. If you'd rather not bow to God, bow to the day. Small, quiet, awake.

wordCard.voice: Surasa. The serpent mother whose test Hanuman passes by shrinking to the size of a thumb, so that her word and his are both kept.

orig.note: Sanskrit buddhi, intelligence or discernment: one of the qualities the gods wanted to see.

carryVoice: Your line: make the ego small: Hanuman bows. The gods saw strength and wisdom both. See you tomorrow.
